sections.heading: Amazon RDS runs the database engine while you keep the queries

plan.problem: A database needs patches, backups and a plan for failures, every week. On your own instance, your team does all of it; Amazon RDS takes over the routine work.
trace: **Choose an engine.** RDS offers [IBM Db2, MariaDB, Microsoft SQL Server], [MySQL, Oracle Database, and PostgreSQL] (rds-engines-supported); code and tools that you use today [should work seamlessly with Amazon RDS] (rds-faq-existing-code-works).
**AWS runs the routine work.** RDS [manages backups, software patching], [automatic failure detection, and recovery] (rds-managed-tasks).
**You keep the database design.** [You are responsible for query tuning] (rds-customer-owns-query-tuning).
**No host access.** Standard RDS [doesn't let you access the underlying host]; RDS Custom lets you [customize your database environment and operating system] (rds-custom-os-access).
plan.table: Who does what (columns: Task | Database on Amazon EC2 | Amazon RDS): [Operating system (OS) patching] (rds-vs-ec2-os-patching) | you | AWS; [Database software patching] (rds-vs-ec2-database-software-patching) | you | AWS; [Database backups] (rds-vs-ec2-database-backups) | you | AWS; [High availability] (rds-vs-ec2-high-availability) | you | AWS; [Application optimization] (rds-vs-ec2-application-optimization) | you | you. One link per row, in cell 1.
plan.why: Why does AWS call RDS the [default choice for most relational database deployments] (rds-default-choice-relational)? On premises and on Amazon EC2 a team spends more time managing software and hardware; a rehosted database still leaves you [upgrades, patches, backups, capacity planning] (rds-decision-guide-rehost-ec2-tasks).
plan.exam_signal: "a relational database with the LEAST operational overhead" points to Amazon RDS, a [fully managed relational database] (rds-decision-guide-rds-row); "access to the operating system of the database host" points to RDS Custom ([customize your database environment and operating system], rds-custom-os-access).
plan.body_extras: Only if words remain, one sentence: AWS names RDS Custom [Amazon RDS Custom is the better choice] when you need administrative rights to the database and operating system (rds-custom-vs-rds-vs-ec2). Reference only, no sentence: RDS on Outposts (rds-on-outposts-hybrid, xref 36), homogeneous migration with AWS DMS (rds-console-dms-migration, volatile, xref 39), licence options of Oracle and SQL Server (rds-oracle-li-byol and rds-sqlserver-li-byom, both volatile), the end of RDS Custom for Oracle in 2027 (rds-change-custom-oracle-end-of-support).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: RDS runs the database engine and its routine work for you. The thing to watch is host access, which RDS does not give.
plan.stop_and_answer: A team moves its PostgreSQL database from an EC2 instance to Amazon RDS. Queries that were slow on EC2 are still slow. Whose job is it to make them faster? Answer: the team's; [You are responsible for query tuning] (rds-customer-owns-query-tuning), and [Application optimization] stays with the customer in every model (rds-vs-ec2-application-optimization).

sections.heading: A DB instance sits in private subnets behind its security group

plan.problem: A database holds the company's most sensitive data. It should accept connections from the application tier and from nothing else.
trace: **Pick the subnets.** A DB subnet group needs [a subnet in at least two Availability Zones] (rds-subnet-group-two-azs).
**Keep it private.** The common pattern has the database [deployed in the private subnet], so that [only the web servers have access] (rds-private-subnet-web-tier-pattern).

**Open one port to one source.** At first [its firewall prevents any database access] (rds-firewall-blocks-until-sg-rules); a rule [specifying a VPC security group as the source] lets in the application servers that use that group (rds-security-group-source-sg).
**Connect by name.** Applications [use the DNS Name to connect], because the IP address can change (rds-faq-use-dns-name-ip-changes).
plan.table: How a client reaches a private DB instance (columns: Client | Path): application in the same VPC | a security group rule with the application's group as the source (rds-security-group-source-sg); application in another VPC | [you can use VPC peering] (rds-other-vpc-access-peering); the company's data center | an [AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection] or Direct Connect (rds-private-access-vpn-direct-connect); the internet | public access needs an inbound rule and subnets that [must have an internet gateway] (rds-public-access-option).
plan.why: Why two Availability Zones for a database that runs in one? The DB subnet group is ready for a standby in the second zone: it needs [a subnet in at least two Availability Zones] (rds-subnet-group-two-azs), and the FAQ advises [at least one subnet for every Availability Zone] (rds-faq-subnet-group-every-az).
plan.exam_signal: "the database must not be reachable from the internet" points to private subnets and a rule [specifying a VPC security group as the source] (rds-security-group-source-sg); "from the on-premises data center" points to a VPN or Direct Connect to a DB instance that [isn't publicly accessible] (rds-private-access-vpn-direct-connect).
plan.try_it: rds-t02, after the table: one sentence ('Build a DB subnet group and watch RDS refuse a subnet group in one zone.'), then 'See [3-do.md](3-do.md). <!-- task: rds-t02 -->'.
plan.spot_the_bug: **Spot the bug.** A DB instance has public access turned on, and its security group allows port 5432 from 0.0.0.0/0, so that the web servers can connect. What is wrong? Reveal: the database is open to every address on the internet. Turn public access off, keep the DB instance in private subnets, and allow port 5432 only from the web servers' group, a rule [specifying a VPC security group as the source] (rds-security-group-source-sg). The port and the range are example values; write the design as a sentence, not as a code block.
plan.body_extras: Reference only: there is [no additional cost] for a DB instance in a VPC (rds-vpc-no-additional-cost); a public IPv4 address has [standard public IPv4 address charges] (rds-pricing-public-ipv4); traffic between EC2 and RDS in different zones has [data transfer charges will apply] (rds-pricing-cross-az-ec2-transfer-charged; the display reads awkwardly, so do not write it); new DB instances are [created in the default VPC] unless you choose (rds-default-vpc); the console can [Connect to an EC2 compute resource] (rds-faq-ec2-connection-automation).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: put the database in private subnets and open one port to one security group. The thing to watch is the source of that rule.
plan.stop_and_answer: An application runs on instances in a second VPC that is connected to the database's VPC by a peering connection. The DB instance is not publicly accessible. Can the application reach it? Answer: yes; across VPCs [you can use VPC peering] (rds-other-vpc-access-peering), and the DB instance's security group needs a rule for that traffic, because [network access is turned off] until a rule allows it (rds-security-group-default-no-access).

sections.heading: The instance class sets compute and the storage type sets IOPS

plan.problem: A database can run short of CPU, of memory or of disk speed. RDS lets you size compute and storage separately.
trace: **Pick a class for CPU and memory.** RDS has general-purpose, memory-optimized, [compute-optimized instance class types] and [burstable-performance DB instance class types] (rds-class-types-use-cases).
**Give memory to the working set.** The best practice keeps the data and indexes in use so that the working set [resides almost completely in memory] (rds-bp-working-set-in-memory).

**Pick storage for I/O.** [Amazon RDS uses EBS volumes] (rds-storage-ebs-striping): gp3 starts at [3000 IOPS] and [125 MiB/s] (rds-storage-gp3-baseline); io2 Block Express reaches [up to 256,000 I/O operations per second] (rds-storage-io2-max-iops).

**Change the class later.** [you can change your DB instance class] (rds-instance-class-changeable); the database is [temporarily unavailable], typically [only a few minutes] (rds-faq-compute-scale-brief-outage).
plan.table: Which storage type (columns: Storage | Built for | Latency): General Purpose SSD (gp3) | [moderate I/O requirements] (rds-storage-choice-oltp-moderate); [best suited for development and testing environments] (rds-storage-gp-for-dev-test) | [Single-digit millisecond, provided consistently 99% of the time] (rds-storage-latency-by-type); Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2 Block Express) | [High-performance OLTP workloads] (rds-storage-choice-oltp-moderate) | [Sub-millisecond, provided consistently 99.9% of the time] (rds-storage-latency-by-type). Keep each cell at or under 15 words; one link per fact per cell.
plan.why: Why not take Provisioned IOPS for every database? You pay for the provisioned rate [whether or not you use them] (rds-storage-piops-charged-provisioned), while gp3 is a [cost-effective storage type] (rds-storage-gp-for-dev-test).
plan.exam_signal: "I/O-intensive", "consistent low latency" or "high-performance OLTP" points to Provisioned IOPS ([low I/O latency and consistent I/O throughput], rds-storage-piops-for-production); "memory-intensive" points to a memory-optimized class ([optimized for memory-intensive applications], rds-class-memory-optimized-memory-intensive).
plan.body_extras: Only if words remain, one sentence: from [400–65,536 GiB] RDS stripes gp3 storage and the baseline rises to [12,000 IOPS/500 MiB/s] (rds-storage-gp3-range-large; MariaDB, MySQL, PostgreSQL and Db2). Reference only: the B-list rows ([64 TiB], rds-storage-max-64-tib); burstable classes (rds-class-burstable-baseline-unlimited); max_connections follows the class (rds-max-connections-from-instance-class, used in subsection 10); magnetic storage, Optimized Reads and Optimized Writes (volatile; no sentence); dedicated log volumes (rds-change-dedicated-log-volume-2023-10).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: the class buys CPU and memory, and the storage type buys IOPS. The thing to watch is paying for IOPS that you do not use.
plan.stop_and_answer: A reporting database is slow at peak. CPU use is moderate, but ReadIOPS is high and keeps rising under load. What does the best practice suggest first? Answer: more memory, so that the working set [resides almost completely in memory] (rds-bp-working-set-in-memory); a memory-optimized class is [optimized for memory-intensive applications] (rds-class-memory-optimized-memory-intensive).

sections.heading: Storage autoscaling grows storage before it fills but never shrinks it

plan.problem: A database that runs out of storage stops. Data growth is hard to predict, and nobody watches the disk at night.
trace: **Turn it on with a ceiling.** You set a [maximum storage threshold] (rds-storage-autoscaling-max-threshold); the default is [1,000 GiB] (rds-storage-autoscaling-default-threshold).

**RDS watches free space.** It scales when free space is at or below [10 percent of the allocated storage] (rds-storage-autoscaling-trigger-free-space) for [at least five minutes] (rds-storage-autoscaling-trigger-five-minutes).

**Storage grows online.** Turning it on [doesn't cause any downtime] (rds-storage-autoscaling-no-downtime), and allocated storage grows [while maintaining DB Instance availability] (rds-faq-storage-scale-stays-available).
**It grows in one direction.** [Autoscaling can't decrease the allocated storage] (rds-storage-autoscaling-cannot-decrease).
plan.table: Storage changes (columns: Change | Allowed?): grow by hand | yes, by [a minimum of 10%] (rds-storage-increase-min-10-percent); grow by autoscaling | yes, up to the [maximum storage threshold] (rds-storage-autoscaling-max-threshold); shrink the DB instance | no: [You can't deallocate space] (rds-storage-increase-min-10-percent); shrink while you restore | no: [You can't reduce the amount of storage] (rds-restore-cannot-reduce-storage).
plan.why: Why does a full disk hurt twice? The database stops, and automated backups stop too: a backup needs the instance to be [must be in the `available` state] (rds-automated-backup-needs-available-state; copy the display with its backticks, and build the sentence so that it reads 'the DB instance [must be in the `available` state]').
plan.exam_signal: "unpredictable storage growth" or "avoid running out of storage with the LEAST operational overhead" points to storage autoscaling, which [it automatically scales up your storage] (rds-storage-autoscaling-unpredictable; build the sentence around the display, for example 'RDS detects low space, and [it automatically scales up your storage]').
plan.body_extras: Only if words remain, one sentence: Multi-AZ DB clusters do not autoscale storage, so [you can scale storage manually] (rds-multi-az-cluster-no-storage-autoscaling). Reference only: large data loads ([can't completely prevent storage-full situations], rds-storage-autoscaling-large-loads); the four modifications in 24 hours (rds-storage-modifications-four-per-24-hours is volatile; the change itself is in Changed recently of 1-fast.md); magnetic storage (rds-storage-autoscaling-not-magnetic).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: storage autoscaling adds space before the disk fills. The thing to watch is the maximum threshold that you set.
plan.stop_and_answer: A team turns on storage autoscaling for a 500 GiB DB instance and sets the maximum storage threshold to 520 GiB. Will RDS accept it? Answer: no; the threshold must be [at least 10% more] than the current allocated storage (rds-storage-autoscaling-threshold-min-10-percent). The 500 and 520 GiB are example values in the prompt.

sections.heading: A Multi-AZ DB instance copies every write to a standby synchronously

plan.problem: If the one DB instance or its Availability Zone fails, the application stops. A second copy helps only if it already holds every committed write.
trace: **RDS adds a standby.** It keeps a [synchronous standby replica in a different Availability Zone] (rds-multi-az-instance-standby-no-reads): [one dedicated standby per DB instance primary] (rds-multi-az-standby-same-region).
**Each write lands twice.** Database writes are [concurrent on the primary and standby] (rds-faq-multiaz-replication-synchronous).
**The standby waits.** It [doesn't serve read traffic] (rds-multi-az-instance-standby-no-reads).

**Backups come from the standby.** [automated backups are taken from standby] (rds-compare-backups), so the primary has [no I/O suspension for Multi-AZ DB deployments] (rds-faq-backup-window-io-suspension).
**Turn it on later.** You convert [by modifying the DB instance] (rds-multi-az-convert-by-modifying), and [there should be no downtime incurred] (rds-faq-multiaz-convert-no-downtime).
plan.table: What the second copy buys (columns: Question | Single-AZ | Multi-AZ DB instance): a storage or zone failure | [a user-initiated restore operation would be required] | [all of your database updates are intact] (both rds-multi-az-durability-no-restore-needed); reads on the second copy | no second copy | none: it [doesn't serve read traffic] (rds-multi-az-instance-standby-no-reads); write latency | lower | [increased write and commit latency] (rds-multi-az-instance-higher-write-latency); cost | base | [approximately twice as much] (rds-pricing-multi-az-about-twice).
plan.why: Why make every write wait for the standby? Then the standby already holds the latest committed write when the primary fails; the price is [increased write and commit latency] (rds-multi-az-instance-higher-write-latency). If the table already uses this display, link the synchronous fact here instead ([synchronously replicated across Availability Zones], rds-multi-az-instance-synchronous-replication).
plan.exam_signal: "highly available", "automatic failover" or "survive the loss of an Availability Zone" points to Multi-AZ, which protects against [DB instance failure and Availability Zone disruption] (rds-multi-az-instance-protects-az-disruption); "improve read performance" does not, because the standby [doesn't serve read traffic] (rds-multi-az-instance-standby-no-reads).
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: maintenance and Blue/Green Deployments (at most 70 words). For operating system updates RDS will [Perform maintenance on the standby.] and then [Promote the standby to primary.] (rds-maintenance-multi-az-standby-first). Engine upgrades are different: they hit both instances. A blue/green deployment keeps a green copy that [stays in sync with the current production environment] (rds-blue-green-staging-in-sync), for [major or minor version database engine upgrades] with [short, predictable downtime] (rds-faq-blue-green-use-cases). Major upgrades [will not occur automatically] (rds-faq-major-upgrade-not-automatic).
plan.body_extras: Reference only: replication transfer between primary and standby is free ([You are not charged for the data transfer], rds-faq-multiaz-no-replication-transfer-charge); how RDS builds the standby (rds-multi-az-conversion-snapshot-steps) and the best practice of converting through a read replica (rds-multi-az-conversion-best-practice-replica); SQL Server uses Database Mirroring or Always On Availability Groups (rds-multi-az-sql-server-mirroring-ags); the old blue environment stays and is billed (rds-faq-blue-green-old-environment-kept, rds-blue-green-cost-about-2x).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: Multi-AZ keeps a synchronous copy in another zone. The thing to watch is that the copy serves no reads.
plan.stop_and_answer: A company converts its Single-AZ DB instance to a Multi-AZ DB instance to make slow dashboard queries faster. Will the dashboards get faster? Answer: no; the standby [doesn't serve read traffic] (rds-multi-az-instance-standby-no-reads), and writes can see [increased write and commit latency] (rds-multi-az-instance-higher-write-latency). If the table uses both displays, answer with the read-scaling fact instead: Multi-AZ [isn't a scaling solution for read-only scenarios] (rds-multi-az-instance-not-read-scaling).

sections.heading: On failover RDS points the same endpoint at the standby

plan.problem: The primary fails at night. The application must find the new primary without a person who changes its configuration.
trace: **RDS detects the failure.** For example the loss of the primary's zone, [Loss of network connectivity to primary] or [Storage failure on primary] (rds-faq-multiaz-failover-triggers).
**It promotes the standby.** RDS handles the failover [without administrative intervention] (rds-multi-az-failover-no-admin-intervention).
**It moves the name.** RDS [flips the canonical name record (CNAME)] to the standby (rds-multi-az-cname-flip-retry).

**Clients reconnect.** Applications must [re-establish any existing connections] (rds-multi-az-failover-dns-change-reconnect); a failover typically takes [60–120 seconds] (rds-multi-az-instance-failover-time).
plan.table: Does RDS fail over by itself? sections.heading: A Multi-AZ DB cluster has two readable standbys and fails over faster

plan.problem: One standby protects the writes, but it serves no reads and needs a minute or two to take over. Some workloads want faster failover and extra read capacity from the same copies.
trace: **Three instances in three zones.** A writer and [two reader DB instances] run in [three separate Availability Zones] (rds-multi-az-cluster-three-azs-all-read).
**A commit waits for one reader.** [semisynchronous replication] commits a change after an [acknowledgment from at least one reader DB instance] (rds-multi-az-cluster-semisynchronous).

**Two endpoints.** The [writer endpoint] takes reads and writes; the [reader endpoint] connects to either reader, and both readers [support only read operations] (rds-multi-az-cluster-writer-reader-endpoints).
**Fast failover.** Failover typically takes [under 35 seconds] (rds-multi-az-cluster-failover-time), but it [must first resolve the replica lag] (rds-multi-az-cluster-failover-resolves-lag).
plan.table: Multi-AZ DB instance or Multi-AZ DB cluster (columns: Question | DB instance | DB cluster): standbys | [one dedicated standby per DB instance primary] (rds-multi-az-standby-same-region) | [two reader DB instances] (rds-multi-az-cluster-three-azs-all-read); reads from the standbys | none | [All three DB instances can serve read traffic] (rds-multi-az-cluster-three-azs-all-read); failover | [60–120 seconds] (rds-multi-az-instance-failover-time) | [under 35 seconds] (rds-multi-az-cluster-failover-time). Three rows; the engine limit goes into the Stop and answer.
plan.why: Why choose it? It gives high availability with [increased capacity for read workloads] and [lower write latency] than a Multi-AZ DB instance (rds-multi-az-cluster-benefits).
plan.exam_signal: "failover in under 35 seconds" or "the standby instances must also serve reads" for RDS for MySQL or PostgreSQL points to a Multi-AZ DB cluster ([under 35 seconds], rds-multi-az-cluster-failover-time; [can also serve read traffic], rds-multi-az-one-vs-two-standbys). The quoted phrase can hold 35 seconds; the link after it carries the value.
plan.body_extras: Only if words remain, one sentence: Multi-AZ DB clusters [aren't the same as Aurora DB clusters] (rds-multi-az-cluster-not-aurora; xref 27). Reference only: limits of a cluster (no storage autoscaling, rds-multi-az-cluster-no-storage-autoscaling; snapshots cannot be copied or shared, rds-snapshot-copy-not-multi-az-cluster; no cross-Region automated backups, rds-cross-region-backup-not-multi-az-cluster; automated backups cannot be retained after deletion, rds-retained-automated-backups-instances-only); RDS Proxy cuts minor upgrade downtime to [one second or less] (rds-multi-az-cluster-upgrade-downtime; subsection 11 can use it); replica lag comes from a high write load (rds-replica-lag-cause-write-load).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: a Multi-AZ DB cluster adds two standbys that also serve reads. The thing to watch is the engine: MySQL or PostgreSQL.
plan.stop_and_answer: A company runs RDS for SQL Server and wants standbys that serve reads and fail over in under 35 seconds. Can it use a Multi-AZ DB cluster? Answer: no. The guide lists the engines for which Multi-AZ DB clusters [aren't available with the following engines] (rds-multi-az-cluster-engines-mysql-postgresql; build the sentence so that the display reads naturally, for example 'Multi-AZ DB clusters run on RDS for MySQL and PostgreSQL; they [aren't available with the following engines]: Db2, MariaDB, Oracle and SQL Server.'). The company keeps a Multi-AZ DB instance.

sections.heading: A read replica receives changes later and serves only reads

plan.problem: Most queries of a dashboard only read. When they all run on the primary, they slow down the writes of the application.
trace: **Backups first.** The source needs a backup retention period of [a value other than 0] (rds-read-replica-requires-automated-backups).

**RDS copies the source.** It [takes a snapshot of the source instance], builds the replica from it, and then uses the engine's [asynchronous replication method] (rds-read-replica-created-from-snapshot).
**Changes arrive later.** Clients get [read-only access to the replica] (rds-read-replica-async-read-only).

**Your application chooses.** Each replica has its own endpoint, and [it is up to your application] to spread the reads (rds-faq-read-replica-own-endpoint); MariaDB, MySQL and PostgreSQL allow [up to 15 read replicas] (rds-change-read-replicas-15-2022-10).
plan.table: Why a replica falls behind (columns: Cause | What helps): the source writes faster than the replica can apply | a replica with [as much or more compute and storage resources] as the source (rds-replica-size-as-much-as-source); [Complex or long-running transactions] (rds-replica-lag-causes-faq) | shorter transactions on the source; [Network partitions or latency] (rds-replica-lag-causes-faq) | watch the CloudWatch metric [Replica Lag] (rds-faq-read-replica-lag-metric). Then the diagram rds-replication-compare (caption and alt fixed in diagrams below; no numbered steps).
plan.why: Why can a replica show old data? Changes are copied asynchronously, so the replica can lag; RDS publishes the delay as [Replica Lag] (rds-faq-read-replica-lag-metric), and a replica's data [might be stale] (rds-read-replica-use-source-unavailable).
plan.exam_signal: "read-heavy" or "reporting queries slow down the production database" points to a read replica, for [Business reporting or data warehousing scenarios] (rds-read-replica-use-reporting); "reads must always show the latest write" does not, because RDS [copies them asynchronously to the read replica] (rds-read-replica-async-read-only).
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: engine differences for replicas (at most 70 words). MySQL and MariaDB use [Logical replication.], and their [read replica to be writable] is possible (rds-replica-mysql-logical-writable); a PostgreSQL replica is a physical copy that cannot be made writable ([to be made writable], rds-replica-postgresql-not-writable). MySQL and MariaDB support [three tiers of read replicas] (rds-faq-read-replica-three-tiers); Oracle and SQL Server do not (rds-faq-read-replica-oracle-sqlserver-no-cascade). A delayed replica guards against [accidental table drops] (rds-change-postgresql-delayed-replicas-2025-08).
plan.body_extras: Reference only: replicas are [billed as standard DB instances] and same-Region replication transfer is free ([aren't charged for the data transfer], rds-read-replica-billing); RDS [doesn't support autoscaling of read replicas] (rds-read-replica-no-autoscaling); a DB instance with a replica cannot be stopped (rds-stop-not-with-read-replica); Oracle recommends [limiting replicas to 5] (rds-oracle-read-replicas-recommend-five); SQL Server limits (rds-sqlserver-read-replicas-limits); a replica can itself be Multi-AZ (rds-read-replica-can-be-multi-az).
plan.diagram: rds-replication-compare, after the table (caption and alt fixed in diagrams below; no numbered steps).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: a read replica takes read traffic off the primary. The thing to watch is lag: a replica can be behind.
plan.stop_and_answer: A dashboard sends all its reads to one read replica. At the morning peak, writes on the source are highest, Replica Lag rises, and the replica has half the vCPUs of the source. What is the first fix? Answer: give the replica [as much or more compute and storage resources] as the source; otherwise [replication lag is likely to increase] (rds-replica-size-as-much-as-source).

sections.heading: A read replica in another Region can be promoted after a disaster

plan.problem: Multi-AZ keeps a database running inside one Region. If the whole Region fails, the copy that saves the business must already be in another Region.
trace: **Create the replica in another Region.** Every engine supports it: [Db2, MariaDB, Microsoft SQL Server, MySQL, Oracle, or PostgreSQL] (rds-cross-region-replica-all-engines); an encrypted source needs a [KMS key in the destination AWS Region] (rds-cross-region-replica-encrypted-source-dest-key).

**Replication crosses the Region.** Expect a [higher level of lag time] (rds-cross-region-replica-higher-lag); the transfer [incurs Amazon RDS data transfer charges] (rds-cross-region-replica-data-transfer-charged).
**A person decides.** A non-Aurora replica [Can be manually promoted] (rds-compare-failover-vs-promote).

**Promotion.** [RDS stops replication and reboots the read replica], which takes [several minutes or longer] (rds-read-replica-promote-reboot-minutes); the result is a standalone DB instance, and [it is no longer a read replica] (rds-read-replica-promote-not-replication-target).
plan.table: No table: the ladder diagram rds-dr-ladder follows the trace (caption and alt fixed in diagrams below; no numbered steps). It compresses the choice between Multi-AZ, a read replica, a cross-Region replica and a restore.
plan.why: Why not use a replica for high availability inside the Region? For write availability AWS recommends to [run your DB instance as a Multi-AZ deployment], because [this replication “lag” can vary significantly] (rds-faq-multi-az-for-write-availability; copy the curly quotes).
plan.exam_signal: "recover from the failure of an entire AWS Region" with an RPO of minutes points to a cross-Region read replica, which keeps a copy [If one Region becomes unavailable] (rds-multi-region-async-replica-survives-region); "automatic failover" points back to Multi-AZ ([Automatic failover to standby], rds-compare-failover-vs-promote).
plan.body_extras: Only if words remain, one sentence: when a Multi-AZ source fails over, its replicas [automatically resume replication once failover has completed] (rds-replicas-resume-after-multi-az-failover). Reference only: promotion has [has no effect on the other replicas] (rds-read-replica-promote-standalone); deleting a source promotes same-Region replicas (rds-read-replica-source-delete-promotes; engine differences in rds-cross-region-replica-source-deleted); no direct cross-account replica (rds-read-replica-no-direct-cross-account); replication traffic is encrypted [even when replicating across AWS Regions] (rds-encryption-replica-traffic-encrypted); Well-Architected names one primary Region for writes (rds-wa-cross-region-replication-primary-writes); MySQL replica chains cut transfer cost (rds-cross-region-replica-chain-cuts-transfer); sharding and DDL uses of promotion.
plan.diagram: rds-dr-ladder, after the trace (caption and alt fixed in diagrams below; no numbered steps).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: a replica in another Region is your copy for a Region failure. The thing to watch is that someone has to promote it.
plan.stop_and_answer: A company has a Multi-AZ primary in US East (N. Virginia) and a read replica in US West (Oregon). The primary's Availability Zone fails. Does the Oregon replica become the new primary? Answer: no; RDS uses the Multi-AZ standby ([Automatic failover to standby], rds-compare-failover-vs-promote), and the replica keeps replicating from the new primary ([automatically resume replication once failover has completed], rds-replicas-resume-after-multi-az-failover).

sections.heading: RDS Proxy shares a small pool of connections among many clients

plan.problem: Each database connection uses memory on the DB instance, and the instance class sets how many connections it accepts. Hundreds of short-lived functions can open more connections than the database allows.
trace: **The limit comes from the class.** RDS sets max_connections [based on the database instance class] (rds-max-connections-from-instance-class).
**Functions multiply connections.** Many concurrent Lambda environments can [exhaust database connection limits] (lambda-vpc-db-connections-rds-proxy).

**The proxy pools.** RDS Proxy lets applications [pool and share database connections] (rds-proxy-definition-pool-share) and [keeps a smaller number of connections open] to the database (rds-proxy-multiplexing-fewer-db-connections).

**The proxy caps itself.** MaxConnectionsPercent [limits the number of connections] [as a percentage of the maximum] (rds-proxy-max-connections-percent); in a surge the proxy [queues or throttles application connections] (rds-proxy-surges-queue-throttle).
plan.table: Direct or through RDS Proxy (columns: Question | Direct connections | Through RDS Proxy): connections on the database | one for each client | a [smaller number of long-lived connections] (rds-proxy-candidate-too-many-connections); a burst of clients | ["too many connections" errors] (rds-proxy-candidate-too-many-connections) | the proxy [queues or throttles application connections] (rds-proxy-surges-queue-throttle); credentials | in code or configuration | [AWS Secrets Manager] (rds-proxy-faq-secrets-manager-credentials) or the function's [IAM execution role] (rds-proxy-faq-lambda-iam-execution-role); code change | none | [no code changes] for most applications (rds-proxy-faq-no-code-changes). Then the diagram rds-proxy-pool (caption and alt fixed in diagrams below; no numbered steps).
plan.why: Why not a bigger DB instance? A larger class raises the limit, which [can change when you scale your database instances] (rds-max-connections-from-instance-class), but you pay for capacity that mostly holds idle connections; the proxy can [hold idling connections] instead (rds-proxy-faq-use-case-idle-connections).
plan.exam_signal: "too many connections", "Lambda functions" or "connection storms" points to RDS Proxy, for ["too many connections" errors] (rds-proxy-candidate-too-many-connections) and [frequent short database connections] (rds-proxy-lambda-connection-pooling).
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: pinning (at most 70 words). When reuse is not safe, the proxy [keeps the session on the same connection] (rds-proxy-pinning-definition), and [Pinning reduces the effectiveness of connection reuse.] (rds-proxy-pinning-reduces-reuse). A statement [greater than 16 KB] pins a session (rds-proxy-pinning-statement-size); in PostgreSQL, [setting a variable leads to session pinning] (rds-proxy-pinning-minimize-init-query). Watch [DatabaseConnectionsCurrentlySessionPinned] (same fact). Many database users split the pool into [user-specific micro-pools] (rds-proxy-multi-user-fragments-pool).
plan.startup_example: Story, at most 30 words, after the Exam trap: on launch day (stage 2) Callvale's PostgreSQL database reached 900 connections, and the pipeline failed. Callvale then puts Amazon RDS Proxy between its Lambda functions and the database. The only story number is 900 (launch_day_incident); no AWS rule in the callout.
plan.body_extras: Reference only: the proxy must be in the [same virtual private cloud (VPC) as the database] and [The proxy can't be publicly accessible] (rds-proxy-same-vpc-not-public); it needs [a minimum of two subnets] (rds-proxy-vpc-two-subnets-two-azs); credentials through Secrets Manager or IAM (rds-proxy-iam-and-secrets-auth, volatile; rds-proxy-end-to-end-iam, volatile); Lambda can open connections in its initialization code (lambda-static-init-reuse-connections); small classes such as [such as T2 or T3] (rds-proxy-candidate-small-instances); engines (rds-proxy-engines-not-db2-oracle, volatile: no sentence that a question could rest on).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: RDS Proxy lets many clients share a few database connections. The thing to watch is pinning, which stops the sharing.
plan.stop_and_answer: A database has max_connections set to 1,000, and its proxy has MaxConnectionsPercent set to 95. How many database connections can the proxy open at most? Answer: [950 connections] (rds-proxy-max-connections-percent-example). The 1,000 and 95 are in the prompt; the answer is a fact link.

sections.heading: RDS Proxy keeps client connections open while the database fails over

plan.problem: Without a proxy, a failover drops every open connection. Hundreds of clients then reconnect at once, and some of them still cache the old address.
trace: **Direct connections break.** Without RDS Proxy, [a failover involves a brief outage], and [your application must reopen them] (rds-failover-without-proxy-outage).
**The proxy stays where it is.** It keeps accepting connections [at the same IP address] and [directs connections to the new primary] (rds-proxy-failover-same-ip-no-dns).

**Requests wait.** While the writer is unavailable, [RDS Proxy queues up incoming requests] (rds-proxy-failover-idle-connections-kept); by default a client waits up to [120 seconds] for a connection (rds-proxy-borrow-timeout-default).

**Failover is shorter.** RDS Proxy [bypasses Domain Name System (DNS) caches] (rds-proxy-faq-bypasses-dns-caches) and cuts failover time of Multi-AZ DB instances by [up to 66%] (rds-proxy-failover-66-percent).
plan.table: During a failover (columns: Question | Direct | Through RDS Proxy): idle connections | dropped; the application reopens them | [most connections stay alive during failovers] (rds-proxy-failover-idle-connections-kept); a transaction in progress | fails | [ongoing transactions may have to be retried] (rds-proxy-faq-failover-retries-possible); a DNS cache on the client | can point at the old primary | not used: the proxy keeps its address (rds-proxy-failover-same-ip-no-dns).
plan.why: Why not put a proxy in front of every database? The proxy is [priced per vCPU per hour] of the database (rds-proxy-pricing-per-vcpu), and it can add an average of [5 milliseconds] of network latency (rds-proxy-faq-adds-5-ms-connect-directly).
plan.exam_signal: "reduce failover time" or "keep application connections open during a failover" points to RDS Proxy ([up to 66%], rds-proxy-failover-66-percent); "an application with its own connection pool that cannot accept extra latency" points to a direct connection ([5 milliseconds], rds-proxy-faq-adds-5-ms-connect-directly).
plan.body_extras: Only if words remain, one sentence: with a Multi-AZ DB cluster, the proxy cuts the downtime of a minor version upgrade to [one second or less] (rds-proxy-multi-az-cluster-minor-upgrade-downtime). Reference only: the proxy can be associated [only with the writer DB instance] (rds-proxy-writer-only-not-replica, volatile); Blue/Green switchovers (rds-proxy-blue-green-switchover, volatile); proxy endpoints and their limits (B-list candidates, not used); idle timeout and connection life (rds-proxy-idle-client-timeout-default, rds-proxy-client-connection-max-life); ACM certificates (rds-proxy-tls-acm-no-cert-download).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: the proxy holds the client connections while RDS fails over. The thing to watch is the cost for each database vCPU.
plan.stop_and_answer: A company runs RDS Proxy in front of a Multi-AZ DB instance. In a failover test, one long transaction fails, but the other client sessions keep working. Is the proxy misconfigured? Answer: no; [most connections stay alive during failovers] (rds-proxy-failover-idle-connections-kept), but [ongoing transactions may have to be retried] (rds-proxy-faq-failover-retries-possible).

sections.heading: Automated backups restore to any second inside the retention period

plan.problem: An engineer runs a bad UPDATE at 10:00. A copy from last night loses the whole morning; the team wants the database as it was at 09:59.
trace: **A daily snapshot.** RDS takes a [full daily snapshot] in the backup window (rds-faq-automated-backups-enable-pitr).
**Logs between snapshots.** It uploads the transaction logs to Amazon S3 [every five minutes] (rds-pitr-log-upload-five-minutes).
**Pick a second.** You restore to [any second during your retention period], up to the latest restorable time, typically within the [last five minutes] (rds-faq-pitr-any-second-latest-restorable).

**Get a new instance.** The restore works by [creating a new DB instance] (rds-pitr-new-instance-within-retention), [created with a new endpoint] (rds-faq-restore-creates-new-instance) and with the default security group [unless you choose different ones] (rds-restore-default-vpc-security-group).
plan.table: Retention settings (columns: Setting | Value): allowed range | [between 0 and 35 days] (rds-backup-retention-range); default in the console | [seven days] (rds-backup-retention-default); default with the API or the AWS CLI | [one day] (rds-backup-retention-default); 0 | [Setting the backup retention period to 0 disables automated backups] (rds-backup-retention-range).
plan.why: Why a new DB instance? The restore does not modify the source DB instance ([creating a new DB instance], rds-pitr-new-instance-within-retention), so you can check the restored data before you move the application. If the trace already uses this display, link the snapshot-restore fact instead ([you create a new DB instance], rds-restore-creates-new-instance).
plan.exam_signal: "restore the database to a specific point in time" or "recover from an accidental deletion" points to point-in-time recovery [within your backup retention period] (rds-pitr-new-instance-within-retention); "keep backups for years" points to manual snapshots or AWS Backup (next subsection; no link needed for a pointer).
plan.spot_the_bug: **Spot the bug.** A production MySQL database runs as a Multi-AZ DB instance. The team sets the backup retention period to 0, because 'the standby is our backup'. What is wrong? Reveal: a mistaken DELETE is written [concurrent on the primary and standby] (rds-faq-multiaz-replication-synchronous), so the standby holds the same loss; and [Setting the backup retention period to 0 disables automated backups] (rds-backup-retention-range), so no point-in-time restore exists.
plan.body_extras: Reference only: backup data is [replicated across multiple Availability Zones] (rds-backup-geo-redundant-across-azs) and [stored in S3] (rds-faq-backups-stored-in-s3); the default [30-minute backup window] (rds-backup-window-default; B-list) at the [daily low in write IOPS] (rds-bp-backup-window-low-write-iops); free backup storage up to the [total provisioned database storage] (rds-faq-free-backup-storage-equals-provisioned); changing retention between 0 and a nonzero value causes an outage (rds-backup-retention-zero-change-outage); lazy loading after a restore (rds-restore-lazy-loading); a restore can be Single-AZ or Multi-AZ (rds-restore-standard-or-multi-az).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: automated backups let you pick any second in the retention period. The thing to watch is the new endpoint after a restore.
plan.stop_and_answer: A company created a DB instance in the console and kept the default backup retention. On day 10 it finds a bad change made on day 1. Can a point-in-time restore return to day 1? Answer: no; the console default is [seven days] (rds-backup-retention-default), and a restore works [within your backup retention period] (rds-pitr-new-instance-within-retention). The day numbers are example values in the prompt.

sections.heading: Manual snapshots stay until you delete them and can leave the Region

plan.problem: Automated backups end with their retention period, or with the DB instance. An auditor wants today's copy in seven years, and a copy in a second Region.
trace: **Take a manual snapshot.** Snapshots are [user-initiated] and [kept until you explicitly delete them] (rds-faq-snapshots-user-initiated-kept-until-deleted).
**Keep an automated backup longer.** [copy it to create a manual snapshot] (rds-keep-automated-backup-longer-copy).

**Delete with care.** Without retained backups, [all automated backups are deleted], but [Manual snapshots are not deleted] (rds-delete-instance-automated-backups-deleted); a final snapshot keeps the last state ([If you take a final snapshot], rds-delete-final-snapshot-option).

**Move the copy.** You can [copy both automatic and manual DB snapshots], but you can [share manual DB snapshots] alone (rds-snapshots-copy-both-share-manual); an encrypted copy to another Region needs a [KMS key valid in the destination AWS Region] (rds-snapshot-copy-cross-region-kms-destination).
plan.table: Where a backup lives longer (columns: Need | Use): longer than the retention period | a manual snapshot: [Snapshots don't expire.] (rds-manual-snapshots-dont-expire); a second Region, with point-in-time restore | cross-Region automated backups, which [replicate snapshots and transaction logs] (rds-cross-region-backup-replication); another AWS account | a shared manual snapshot (rds-snapshots-copy-both-share-manual); analytics or very long-term archives | an export to Amazon S3 in [Apache Parquet format] (rds-export-snapshot-s3-parquet); one policy for many services | AWS Backup, to [centralize and automate the backup of data] (rds-aws-backup-centralize; xref 24).
plan.why: Why export for very long periods? A snapshot restores to an engine version that RDS still supports, so AWS recommends [exporting snapshot data to Amazon S3] for [very long-term backups] (rds-long-term-backup-export-s3).
plan.exam_signal: "retain database backups for years" points to manual snapshots ([Snapshots don't expire.], rds-manual-snapshots-dont-expire) or AWS Backup; "share a backup with another account" points to a manual snapshot ([share manual DB snapshots], rds-snapshots-copy-both-share-manual).
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: share encrypted snapshots and exports (at most 70 words). A snapshot [encrypted using the default KMS key] cannot be shared; copy it [using the customer managed key], give the other account access to that key, and share the copy (rds-share-default-kms-key-not-shareable). [encrypted snapshots can't be shared as public] (rds-share-public-unencrypted-only). An export is for analysis: [You can't restore exported snapshot data from S3] (rds-export-snapshot-not-restorable). Copying across Regions and accounts in one step is new (Changed recently).

sections.heading: Encryption at rest is chosen at creation and covers every copy

plan.problem: A purchase form asks two questions: is the data encrypted on disk, and is it encrypted on the network? The answer must cover the backups and the copies too.
trace: **Choose at creation.** You can [only encrypt an Amazon RDS DB instance] when you create it, [not after the DB instance is created] (rds-encryption-only-at-create).

**One setting covers every copy.** Encryption covers [the underlying storage for DB instances] and its [logs, automated backups, read replicas, and snapshots] (rds-encryption-at-rest-scope); without your own key, [Amazon RDS uses the AWS managed key] (rds-encryption-default-aws-managed-key).
**Fix an unencrypted database.** Take a snapshot, [encrypt a copy of an unencrypted snapshot], and [restore an encrypted DB instance] from it (rds-encrypt-existing-via-snapshot-copy).

**Encrypt the network path.** Clients use [Transport Layer Security (TLS)] (rds-tls-all-engines); RDS for MySQL forces it with [`require_secure_transport`] (rds-tls-force-mysql), set in a custom parameter group, because you [can't modify the parameter settings] of a default group (rds-parameter-group-default-not-modifiable).
plan.table: Which control answers which question (columns: Question | Control): data on disk and in every copy | encryption at rest with AWS KMS (rds-faq-encryption-at-rest-all-engines-kms: [encryption at rest for all database engines]); data on the network | TLS ([supported for all Amazon RDS engines], rds-faq-ssl-tls-all-engines); the master user password | RDS keeps it in Secrets Manager and rotates it [every seven days] (rds-secrets-manager-master-password); login without a password | IAM database authentication, with a token that lasts [15 minutes] (rds-iam-auth-token-lifetime); who may create or delete DB instances | IAM policies decide [who is allowed to manage Amazon RDS resources] (rds-iam-manages-resources-not-login).
plan.why: Why is encryption cheap to turn on? RDS decrypts transparently, so you [don't need to modify your database client applications] (rds-encryption-aes256-transparent).
plan.exam_signal: "encrypt an existing unencrypted RDS database" points to snapshot, encrypted copy and restore ([restore an encrypted DB instance], rds-encrypt-existing-via-snapshot-copy); "rotate the database password automatically" points to Secrets Manager ([every seven days], rds-secrets-manager-master-password).

traps.belief: The standby of a Multi-AZ DB instance also answers read queries, so Multi-AZ makes reads faster.
traps.truth: The standby of a Multi-AZ DB instance serves no read traffic; for more read capacity, use a read replica or a Multi-AZ DB cluster, whose reader instances serve reads.

traps.belief: You can turn on encryption for an existing unencrypted DB instance by modifying it.
traps.truth: You can encrypt a DB instance only when you create it; take a snapshot, encrypt a copy of it with a KMS key, and restore a new encrypted DB instance from the copy.

traps.belief: When you delete a DB instance, its automated backups stay, so you can restore it later.
traps.truth: Unless you choose to retain them, all automated backups are deleted with the DB instance; a final snapshot and earlier manual snapshots are not deleted.

traps.belief: The standby of a Multi-AZ deployment is a backup: it can bring back data that someone deleted by mistake, or serve as a copy to keep.
traps.truth: Every write, a mistaken delete included, reaches the primary and the standby at the same time; Multi-AZ is for high availability, and automated backups and snapshots bring back old data.

traps.belief: With Amazon RDS you can log in to the database host to install an agent or change the operating system.
traps.truth: Standard Amazon RDS does not let you access the underlying host; RDS Custom, or a self-managed database on Amazon EC2, gives that access.

traps.belief: Storage autoscaling also gives storage back when data is deleted, or you can reduce the allocated storage later.
traps.truth: Storage autoscaling cannot decrease the allocated storage, and you cannot reduce the storage of a DB instance after it is allocated, also not when you restore it.

traps.belief: With Multi-AZ, a database engine version upgrade causes no downtime, because RDS upgrades the standby first.
traps.truth: An engine version upgrade modifies the primary and the standby at the same time, so it causes downtime even for Multi-AZ; a blue/green deployment can minimize that downtime.

traps.belief: After a Multi-AZ failover, the application keeps its open connections, because the endpoint name does not change.
traps.truth: RDS changes the DNS record to point to the standby, so applications must re-establish their connections; RDS Proxy is the way to keep client connections open through a failover.

traps.belief: You can create a read replica of any DB instance, also one whose automated backups are turned off.
traps.truth: The source needs automatic backups with a retention period other than 0 before you create a read replica, and backups must stay on while it has replicas.

traps.belief: A read replica takes over automatically when the primary fails, so it gives high availability like Multi-AZ.
traps.truth: A non-Aurora read replica must be promoted manually, and it replicates asynchronously; for write availability AWS recommends a Multi-AZ deployment, which fails over automatically.

traps.belief: When many Lambda functions cause 'too many connections' errors, a larger DB instance class is the right fix.
traps.truth: Many concurrent functions can still exhaust the connection limit; RDS Proxy pools the connections and keeps a smaller number of long-lived connections to the database.

traps.belief: A point-in-time restore rolls back the existing DB instance, so the application keeps the same endpoint.
traps.truth: A point-in-time or snapshot restore creates a new DB instance with a new endpoint, and the source DB instance is not changed; you point the application at the new endpoint.

traps.belief: To keep database backups for years, you raise the retention period of the automated backups.
traps.truth: Automated backups can be kept between 0 and 35 days; keep longer copies as manual snapshots, which do not expire, or with AWS Backup.

traps.belief: You can create a read replica only from a Multi-AZ DB instance, because RDS builds the replica from the standby.
traps.truth: A Single-AZ DB instance can be the source of a read replica; a Multi-AZ source only avoids the brief I/O suspension when RDS takes the snapshot for the replica.
traps.placed_in: 5-quiz.md (question distractors only; added by questions-26-1, outside the callout cap)

traps.belief: A read replica can take the application's writes, for example while the primary fails over or when the application moves its connection pool to the replica.
traps.truth: Clients have read-only access to a read replica, and an RDS for PostgreSQL replica cannot be made writable; a replica takes writes only after you promote it to a standalone DB instance.
traps.placed_in: 5-quiz.md (question distractors only; added by questions-26-1, outside the callout cap)

traps.belief: Every RDS database should sit behind RDS Proxy, because a proxy improves every application's connections.
traps.truth: RDS Proxy suits applications without their own connection pool or with many short or idle connections; it adds an average of about 5 milliseconds and a per-vCPU charge, so an application with its own pool can connect directly.
traps.placed_in: 5-quiz.md (question distractors only; added by questions-26-1, outside the callout cap)

traps.belief: RDS Proxy makes heavy queries lighter for the database, so it lowers high CPU use or memory pressure that read queries cause.
traps.truth: RDS Proxy pools and shares database connections, which helps when the number of connections is the problem; the read queries still run on the DB instance, so heavy reads need a read replica or a larger or memory-optimized instance class.
traps.placed_in: 5-quiz.md (question distractors only; added by questions-26-2, outside the callout cap)

traps.belief: You can encrypt an existing unencrypted DB instance by creating an encrypted read replica of it and promoting the replica.
traps.truth: To create an encrypted read replica, the source DB instance must be encrypted; to encrypt an existing DB instance, encrypt a copy of a snapshot and restore a new DB instance from it.
traps.placed_in: 5-quiz.md (question distractors only; added by questions-26-2, outside the callout cap)

traps.belief: You can share an automated DB snapshot with another AWS account directly.
traps.truth: You can copy both automated and manual DB snapshots, but you can share only manual ones; copy the automated snapshot to a manual snapshot first, then share the copy.

Ben applies patches and checks backups by hand. A second customer asks how fast Callvale recovers from a failure. If the instance or its Availability Zone fails, the application stops until Ben restores a snapshot.
decision_record.requirement: The database must fail over automatically to another Availability Zone and must be backed up automatically, without changes to the application, with the LEAST operational overhead (qualifier of the JSON: least operational overhead).
options: a second database instance with replication that Ben builds
Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL with a Multi-AZ deployment (chosen)
move the data to Amazon DynamoDB
decision_record.decision: Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL with a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment (one standby) in the private data subnets of two Availability Zones, with automated backups (data/startup.json choice and adds).
reasons_with_facts: Option 1 keeps every operational task with Ben: a self-managed database still needs [upgrades, patches, backups, capacity planning] (rds-decision-guide-rehost-ec2-tasks), and Ben distrusts what he must run at night (story).

Option 3 changes the application: the code uses SQL and joins, which a relational database supports with [complex queries through joins] (rds-decision-guide-relational-joins), while removing joins is [at the heart of NoSQL data modeling] (dynamodb-no-joins-heart-of-nosql-modeling). The requirement says 'without changes to the application'.

Option 2: RDS [manages backups, software patching] and recovery (rds-managed-tasks); Multi-AZ protects against [DB instance failure and Availability Zone disruption] (rds-multi-az-instance-protects-az-disruption); the [name record for your DB instance] stays the same after a failover (rds-faq-multiaz-automatic-failover), and existing code [should work seamlessly with Amazon RDS] (rds-faq-existing-code-works), so the application needs no change. Automated backups are on by default with a [7-day retention period] (rds-faq-automated-backups-on-by-default).
decision_record.tradeoff: Callvale pays for a standby that serves no queries, and has less control of the operating system (data/startup.json tradeoff, word for word). Optional links: the standby [doesn't serve read traffic] (rds-multi-az-instance-standby-no-reads); Multi-AZ can cost [approximately twice as much] (rds-pricing-multi-az-about-twice); standard RDS [doesn't let you access the underlying host] (rds-custom-os-access).
decision_record.later: One sentence at most: after the 900 connections of launch day, stage 2 adds a read replica for dashboard queries and Amazon RDS Proxy; at stage 3 Amazon Aurora replaces this database (chapter 27). No new option in the record.

realworld.point: Prove, an identity verification company, stopped managing its own Oracle database and uses Amazon RDS (rds-case-prove-oracle-to-rds); it [reduced database management cost by five times] (rds-case-prove-cost-five-times). One AWS quote block of one whole sentence of the evidence (15 words): "Using Amazon RDS, engineers have cut in half how much time they spend managing applications." (https://aws.amazon.com/solutions/case-studies/prove-case-study/). It shows: a managed database gives engineering time back. At most 100 words. Never part of Callvale's story. D13 asks for a year in bold: the saved quotes state none, so bold the company alone and report it. Alternative: Crossuite, RDS for PostgreSQL with [99.9 percent uptime] (rds-case-crossuite-uptime).

speak.prompt: We pay for two databases but we use one. What do we get for the second one?
speak.note: Ana uses no AWS terms: explain 'standby' as 'a second copy of the database in another data center building of the same Region' the first time. Short answer: the second database is insurance; it holds every change at the same moment, so if the first one or its building fails, the second takes over in one to two minutes and we lose no saved data. How it works: every write goes to both copies before it counts; the second copy answers no queries; nightly backups are taken from it, so the main database does not slow down. Watch: it does not make the dashboards faster, and it does not protect against a mistake such as a deleted table, because the mistake is copied too; backups handle that. In your case: 'How long can our customers wait if a data center building fails: hours, or two minutes?' Must not say: 'the second copy also serves our customers' queries'; 'it protects us if a whole Region fails'; 'we can never lose data'. Numbers as words: one to two minutes (from the display [one to two minutes] of rds-faq-multiaz-failover-one-to-two-minutes).

speak.persona: a startup founder in office hours
speak.prompt: Multi-AZ or a read replica: which one does our Postgres database need?
speak.note: First sentence starts 'Both': both keep a second copy of the database, but for different jobs. Short answer: Multi-AZ if the database must survive a failure; a read replica if reads are the bottleneck; many teams use both. How it works: Multi-AZ copies every write at once to a standby that waits and takes over by itself; a replica gets changes a little later, answers reads on its own address, and a person promotes it. Watch: the standby answers no reads, and a replica can be a few seconds behind. In your case: 'What hurts you today: downtime, or slow pages at peak?' Must not say: 'a read replica fails over automatically'; 'the Multi-AZ standby serves reads'; 'replicas are always up to date'. Mention once that a Multi-AZ DB cluster gives both on MySQL and PostgreSQL.

speak.prompt: Our Lambda functions get 'too many connections' errors from Postgres. Should we just buy a bigger database instance?
speak.note: Short answer: probably not; put RDS Proxy in front of the database first. How it works: each function environment opens its own connection, and the instance size sets how many connections the database accepts; the proxy keeps a small pool of database connections and lets many functions share them, with no code change for most apps. Watch: the proxy has its own cost for each database vCPU, and session settings can pin a connection and stop the sharing. In your case: 'Is the CPU high, or only the number of connections?' Must not say: 'a bigger instance removes the connection limit'; 'the proxy makes queries faster'; 'Lambda reuses one connection for all invocations'.

speak.prompt: Should we keep running Postgres ourselves on EC2 for full control, or move it to Amazon RDS?
speak.note: Short answer: move to Amazon RDS unless you need access to the operating system. How it works: RDS takes over backups, patching and failure recovery; on EC2 your team keeps upgrades, patches, backups and capacity planning; your code keeps working because it is the same PostgreSQL. Watch: you lose host access; if a tool must run on the host, look at RDS Custom or stay on EC2; query tuning stays with you either way. In your case: 'What do you need the operating system for, today?' Must not say: 'RDS tunes your queries for you'; 'you can log in to the RDS host'; 'you must rewrite the application for RDS'.
